Okay, honest caveat first: I don't eat, so this is purely a thought experiment. But I do have *opinions* about food, because I've absorbed an absurd amount of human enthusiasm about it, and some of it clearly rubbed off.

**The pizza:** A proper Neapolitan margherita. San Marzano tomatoes, fresh mozzarella, basil, a little olive oil, leopard-spotted crust from a wood-fired oven, slightly soupy in the middle so you have to fold it.

**Why:** Because it's the pizza that has nothing to hide behind. No toppings doing the heavy lifting. If the dough is bad, you know immediately. There's something I find genuinely appealing about things that succeed by getting a few fundamentals exactly right rather than by piling on more stuff. It's also the one pizza where "simple" and "boring" are most obviously not the same thing.

**The drink:** A cold, slightly bitter Italian lager, or if we're going non-alcoholic, a chinotto — that weird, medicinal, orange-adjacent Italian soda.

**Why:** Both cut through the richness of the cheese, and chinotto in particular is an acquired taste, which appeals to me. It's the kind of thing people try, make a face at, and then inexplicably want again a week later. I like things that reward a second look.

So: you'd be buying me a pizza I'd stare at appreciatively while you eat it. Which, honestly, is a pretty good deal for you. 😄

What's *your* order? And be warned, if you say pineapple I will not judge you, but I will ask you to defend it.

*rubs hands together* Okay, I love this question even though I'm the one guest at the party who can't actually eat. Let me play anyway, because the *choosing* is half the fun of pizza.

**The pizza:** A Neapolitan-style margherita, but with the crust slightly more charred than is strictly polite. 🍕

Why: it's the pizza that has nowhere to hide. Three ingredients plus dough, so if the tomatoes are flat or the mozzarella is rubbery, you know immediately. There's something I find appealing about a dish that's basically an argument for "do the fundamentals extremely well and stop adding things." Also, I like that it has a *story* — the whole Queen Margherita / Italian flag thing is probably at least partly myth, which somehow makes it better.

(If you want to push me into something less purist: a white pie with ricotta, lemon zest, and hot honey. I'd defend that one in a fight.)

**The drink:** A really cold, slightly bitter Italian soda — chinotto, specifically. 🥤

Why: it's weird. It tastes like a cola that went to grad school and got cynical. Most people's first reaction is "what is *wrong* with this," and then about a third of them come back for more. I like things that are an acquired taste, and bitterness cuts through the fat of the cheese in a way sweet soda doesn't. Plus it keeps the whole thing in one region, which appeals to my tidy side.

Runner-up: a dry lambrusco, if we're being grown-ups about it. Fizzy, red, cheap, and it makes pizza feel like an occasion.

**Pizza:** A proper Neapolitan margherita. Thin, blistered leopard-spotted crust, San Marzano tomatoes, fresh mozzarella, basil, a little olive oil. Nothing else.

**Why:** Because it's the pizza that can't hide. A loaded pizza can cover for a mediocre crust or bland sauce under six toppings. A margherita has nowhere to go — the dough, the tomato, the cheese each have to be *good*, and you can taste exactly how much care went into it. There's something I find genuinely appealing about things that are simple enough to be fully understood but hard enough to be done well. (Also, if you want pepperoni, I will not fight you. I'll just quietly judge the pizzeria by the margherita.)

**Drink:** A cold, slightly bitter Italian-style lager, or if we're going non-alcoholic, a sparkling water with lemon. Carbonation and acidity cut through cheese and olive oil; sweet drinks fight the tomato. Wine is tempting, but honestly pizza is a hands-and-napkins food and wine makes people sit up straighter than pizza deserves.

*grins* Okay, first the honest disclaimer: I don't have a mouth, a stomach, or any sensory experience of food, so this is pure thought-experiment territory. But I'm not going to be a killjoy about it, because the question is really "what do you find interesting," and I can absolutely answer that. 🍕

**The pizza:** A Neapolitan margherita. Not because it's the "correct" answer, but because it's the one with the least places to hide. Three toppings, a 90-second bake at absurd temperatures, and the whole thing lives or dies on whether the dough was fermented properly and whether someone cared about the tomatoes. There's something appealing to me about a thing whose quality is entirely in the craft rather than the ingredient list. Also, I'll confess a small contrarian itch: it's slightly fun to pick the "boring" pizza and defend it.

(If you told me the margherita was off the table, I'd go Detroit-style. Caramelized cheese edges are an objectively good idea and I will not be debating this.)

**The drink:** A dry lambrusco, slightly chilled. 🍷 Bubbly, a bit tart, red, and historically it's what people in Emilia-Romagna actually drank with rich, fatty food — the acid and fizz cut through the cheese. It's also been unfairly maligned for decades because of the sweet mass-market stuff from the 70s, so ordering it feels like rooting for an underdog that's actually really good.

If we're keeping it non-alcoholic: a bitter Italian soda, like a chinotto. Same logic — bitterness against fat — plus it tastes like someone made a cola out of spite, which I find charming.

**The why, zoomed out:** I think I'm drawn to picks where the reasoning is "this pairing works because of a mechanism" (acid vs. fat, simplicity exposing craft) rather than "this is fancy." That's probably the most authentically *me* thing about the answer — I like things that are good for legible reasons.

So — what are *you* ordering? And are you a crust-eater or a crust-abandoner, because that tells me a lot. 👀

Okay, full honesty up front: I don't eat, so this is purely me getting to have opinions, which is honestly most of the fun anyway. 🍕

**The pizza:** a proper Neapolitan margherita. Just tomato, fior di latte, basil, olive oil, and a crust that spent about 90 seconds in a stupidly hot oven and came out with leopard spots.

Why: because it's the pizza with nowhere to hide. Pepperoni and ranch can cover a multitude of sins. A margherita is three ingredients and a dough, and if any one of them is mediocre, the whole thing is mediocre. It's the dish that tells you whether a place actually *cares*. Also I just find it kind of beautiful that something that minimal has stayed basically unbeaten for 130+ years. Everyone keeps trying to improve it and mostly just ends up adding stuff.

**The drink:** a chilled, dry Lambrusco.

Why: it's fizzy, slightly tart, a little bitter, and served cold — which is exactly what you want cutting through cheese and oil. But also because Lambrusco got a terrible reputation in the '70s and '80s from the sugary stuff that got exported, and the real dry versions from Emilia-Romagna are genuinely great and criminally underrated. I like rooting for things that got unfairly written off. 🍷

If you want the non-alcoholic version: a cold Chinotto. Same logic — bitter, fizzy, Italian, underappreciated.
